picked.t: Nhaan Resort & Spa Hoi An introduces riverside seafood restaurant Plait
picked.body: Located along the Co Co River, Plait sources seafood from local suppliers, including Duy Hai Fish Market in Hoi An. Depending on the daily catch and season, selections may include golden rabbitfish, silver pomfret and moray eel. Diners can choose their seafood and preparation method, including charcoal grilling in a Josper oven or hot-pot cooking. Executive chef Duong Danh Linh, who grew up in central Vietnam, leads the restaurant's culinary program, which combines regional ingredients with traditional cooking methods. Plait also offers cooking classes through the resort's "Meet the Artisans" program, which introduces guests to local crafts and traditions through experiences with artisans from Thanh Ha Pottery Village and Kim Bong Carpentry Village. For the cooking classes, guests visit a local market with the chef in the morning to learn about seasonal produce and seafood brought in by fishing boats. Back at the resort, they take part in a "No Menu" session, preparing dishes based on the ingredients available that day before enjoying their meals at Plait. Signature dishes include Tan Thanh squid seared on volcanic stone and Ninh Hoa Babylon snails flambéed at the table. Yellowfin tuna from Phu Yen is dry-aged before grilling, while whole fish can be baked in clay and opened at the table. Other options include raw and chilled seafood, wok-fried dishes, Quang Nam tiger prawns, Binh Ba lobster and wagyu beef. The menu also features oyster congee and desserts inspired by local specialties, including Hoi An-style tau pho , a traditional tofu pudding. The beverage menu includes cocktails inspired by the town's landscape and culture, such as Lantern Glow, referencing its lantern-lit streets, and Garden Breeze, inspired by its gardens and natural surroundings. Sridhar Thota, general manager of Nhaan Resort & Spa Hoi An, said Plait aims to introduce visitors to Central Vietnamese cuisine through locally sourced ingredients and interactive dining. "At Nhaan Resort & Spa Hoi An, we empower travelers to explore the rich cultural traditions of central Vietnam. Plait brings the restaurant's vision to life with an interactive approach to gastronomy, where our chefs showcase Central Vietnamese cuisine and elevate it with contemporary techniques," he said. Plait is one of four dining venues at the resort, alongside Keng, an all-day dining restaurant; Bong Lounge, a riverside bar; and Nipa Pool Bar, which offers poolside dining. Located in Vong Nhi Village, about five kilometers from Hoi An Ancient Town and 750 meters from Cua Dai Beach, the resort has 174 rooms and suites. Designed by Vietnamese architect Vo Trong Nghia, the property draws on the area's traditional architecture and the craftsmanship of Kim Bong Carpentry Village. Its facilities include an outdoor swimming pool, an eforea spa and health club, meeting and event spaces, and activities introducing guests to local traditions. Nhaan Resort & Spa Hoi An is part of Tapestry Collection by Hilton, a portfolio of hotels and resorts with individual identities shaped by their destinations. For more information about Plait or reservations, visit the resort's official website or email dadha_reservations@hilton.com.

picked.t: South Korea's top university considers $748 monthly stipend, free tuition for first foreign-only class
picked.body: "Because we expect to select only a small number of students initially, we are preparing to provide scholarships to all of them," Noh Yoo-sun, the SNU College dean overseeing the launch of the Global Talent Division, told The Korea Herald . Under the plan, students would receive the support for roughly their first three semesters, a period Noh described as "incubation" before they enter their majors. The division will admit international students without requiring them to declare a major. Students are expected to spend about two to three semesters on intensive Korean-language and foundational courses before moving into eligible majors across 10 colleges. "The amount has not been finalized yet," Noh said. "What we are currently considering is full tuition and 1 million won a month in living expenses." SNU expects a first cohort of about 36 students but will set no fixed quota, he said, with the final number depending on the size of the applicant pool and how many candidates the university considers sufficiently qualified. Noh said student support, including scholarships, can play a decisive role in the competition for top students, citing Vietnamese students admitted to SNU who chose the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) instead. About nine students have made a similar choice, he said. "If we want to attract outstanding students, what the university can offer those students becomes very important," he said. He acknowledged that offering the division's students better scholarships than other international students admitted through SNU's special admissions for foreigners could raise fairness concerns. SNU is also considering charging students in the division higher tuition than Korean students, partly because they will receive extra support such as intensive Korean-language classes and one-on-one peer tutoring, Noh said. The amount has not been set and would need approval through the university's tuition-setting process. If the scholarship package is finalized, however, the first cohort would have its tuition fully covered during the premajor period. Noh said SNU is still building the systems needed to recruit, teach and support more international undergraduates, including stronger Korean-language instruction, tailored foundational courses and better access to housing and other student services. The university expects the division to expand as those systems become established, he said. The scholarship model is likely to change as the division grows. Noh said SNU may eventually offer different levels of support or limit scholarships to selected students rather than the whole cohort. SNU is targeting Vietnam as one of five priority recruitment markets for the division, alongside mainland China, Taiwan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, Korea JoongAng Daily reported in October. SNU College faculty and staff are scheduled to visit Vietnam in January 2027 to present admissions guidelines, the newspaper said. Applicants and both their parents must be foreign nationals, according to SNU's admissions office. The scholarship plan is part of SNU's push to attract stronger international applicants and raise its relatively small number of international undergraduates. The university placed 38th in the 2027 QS World University Rankings, the highest of any South Korean university. Vietnamese students became the largest group of international students in South Korean higher education this year, making up 31.5% of 307,464 and overtaking Chinese students for the first time, according to Education Ministry data released in August.

picked.t: Atlas Air could double Vietnam operations if infrastructure improves: CEO
picked.body: "We could probably double the size of our operation here over the next several years," Steen told VnExpress International. The U.S.-based company has recorded 1,269 flight movements in Vietnam so far this year, up over 3,200% from 2016. It runs about 12 weekly frequencies to Hanoi. Steen said that level of activity is probably close to the maximum the existing infrastructure can handle, even though demand could support further growth. Atlas needs more parking stands that can accommodate large freighters such as the Boeing 747-8, along with warehouses and ground handling capacity to prepare pallets and containers for export. Digital platforms for exchanging transport documents and other shipment information are also essential, he said. While new facilities are being built, Vietnam could make better use of existing capacity by improving coordination, communication and operational planning. "You can always optimize utilization of existing infrastructures," Steen said. On the demand side, expanding manufacturing creates more business for operators connecting Vietnam’s factories with overseas markets. Atlas bases its deployment decisions on where manufacturers and customers need capacity. "Manufacturing is always going to attract logistics providers," Steen said. AI investment and data-center construction are adding to that demand, creating time-sensitive shipments of semiconductors and other high-value electronic components. "Components for data centers are being manufactured in Vietnam and other Southeast Asian destinations and then flown into the U.S. for final assembly," he said. Most freight on Atlas’ Vietnam operations consists of high-tech products, Steen said, naming HP and Dell among the manufacturers. Through July, Atlas carried 39% of cargo flown nonstop from Vietnam to the U.S. by American carriers. Vietnam’s broader air cargo market is also expanding. Cargo throughput at Vietnamese airports reached approximately 1.6 million tonnes in the first 10 months, up 9.6% from the same period last year, according to the Civil Aviation Authority of Vietnam (CAAV). Although air cargo represents a small share of total freight volume, it accounts, on average, for about 30% of the value of Vietnam’s imports and exports across all transport modes, the authority said. To accommodate growing demand, Vietnam is investing in new airports that could help ease the capacity constraints Steen described. "Vietnam is doing a lot of the right things at the moment," he said. "Putting capital into infrastructure is absolutely critical, both on the passenger side as well as the cargo side." In the south, Long Thanh International Airport is expected to begin commercial operations on Dec. 24, 2026, according to plans reported by the Airports Corporation of Vietnam and the CAAV. Its first phase is designed to handle 1.2 million tonnes of cargo annually. In the north, Gia Binh International Airport is targeting commercial operations by the end of 2028 and is planned to handle 1.6 million tonnes of cargo a year by 2030. "It’s going to help us as operators operate more effectively and efficiently," Steen said of infrastructure investment. "It’s going to help us add more capacity."
